title: Holloway Systems — Airwall staging, KV prefetch & batch/quant tuning
summary: Deep technical sync focused on air-gapped artifact staging, offline licensing activation flow, KV cache warmup strategy, batching defaults and quantization profile tradeoffs for Holloway's on-prem inference cluster. Agreed on pilot acceptance criteria and next steps for driver signing and a small throughput benchmark.
topics: Security controls: KMS/HSM, audit logs, SSO
action_items: Maya Chen; Share signed artifact transfer checklist + secure MD5 manifest; 2026-06-22
Liam Ortega; Provide baseline bench script (short seq=128, long seq=1024) and recommended batching params; 2026-06-20
Raj Patel; Confirm airwall window and list of hosts for bundle sync; 2026-06-21
Sasha Ivanov; Upload sample model artifact (~4.2GB) to staging and confirm checksum; 2026-06-24
Dana Park; Send security questionnaire answers and KMS key policy draft; 2026-06-25
next_steps: Redwood to deliver a signed installer bundle and offline activation token instructions
Customer to allocate 3 nodes for pilot and run Redwood bench script
Schedule follow-up 30-min checkpoint week after pilot start
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Alright, hey everyone, thanks for making time. We're on for about an hour, wanted to go deep on the airwall staging plan and the runtime perf knobs that Sash a and Raj raised.
[00:10] Raj (Holloway - Lead SRE): Yeah thanks, Maya. We've got a 3-node test cluster ready, 4xA100-ish equivalent, and we'll be using our internal package transport. We need to validate drivers, the offline license activation and then run a couple throughput and tail-latency checks.
[00:25] Liam (Redwood SE): Great. Quick intro — I'm Liam, I run performance at Redwood, I can walk through KV prefetch and batching heuristics and how quantization affects latency.
[00:33] Sasha (Holloway - ML Infra): Hey all, Sasha here. Primary ask: we saw token-level slowdowns when we tried a 2k sequence earlier, and we're trying to tune the KV warmup and batching to keep p95 under 400ms for typical 256-512 seqs.
[00:48] Dana (Holloway - Security): And from security side, we need to make sure offline activation uses KMS-wrapped tokens and audit logs are preserved. Also SOC 2 controls around artifact delivery.
[00:59] Maya: Perfect. We'll go in order — artifact delivery, offline licensing workflow, GPU drivers, then runtime tuning: KV, batching, quant.
[01:08] Tom (Holloway - Infra Ops): Quick logistics note — our airwall only allows USB-validated bundle ingestion or a signed rsync over an internal transfer host. We need to be explicit about file signatures, checksum and the manifest format.
[01:20] Maya: Absolutely. We'll supply a signed manifest, SHA-256 and MD5 for parity; also a signature file using our release key. Note: sometimes the signature verification tool reports 'unknown key' if the bundle metadata is parsed differently, we've seen that with other customers.
[01:34] Raj: Good, call that out. Also driver packaging — we run a custom kernel (5.15) so kernel module compatibility is a concern.
[01:42] Liam: For drivers, two paths: pre-built signed kernel modules for your kernel version, or a small build artifact and a build script we run inside your airgap to compile modules locally. The latter reduces the need for kernel-module signing but requires our compile toolchain. Which do you prefer?
[01:58] Tom: Prefer pre-built if possible, but we don't want unsigned modules. Do you sign modules?
[02:04] Maya: We can provide signed modules. We also provide a signed installer that verifies module signatures against our vendor cert. We'll include a module signature chain and verify steps in the checklist.
[02:13] Dana: That helps from the compliance perspective. Also, how does the offline licensing handshake work? We need to ensure there's no plaintext token transit via removable media.
[02:22] Priya (Redwood Support): For offline licensing, the flow is: we generate an activation blob tied to your cluster id (hash of hostnames+macs), you import via the secure ingest path, then run an activation tool that talks to our offline license verifier inside the cluster — it's all local. The activation blob itself is KMS-wrapped so only your HSM/KMS can unwrap.
[02:39] Sasha: Can you clarify "cluster id"? Are we comfortable with MAC addresses as identifiers? We have ephemeral hosts sometimes.
[02:46] Liam: Good point. We recommend a signing profile that uses a persistent machine UUID or a provided cluster fingerprint file created during provisioning. Works even if you rotate NICs.
[02:55] Raj: Ok we'll provide a persistent fingerprint.
[02:58] Maya: Next, KV cache warming — Sasha, you mentioned cold p95 spikes at long sequences. Can you walk through your workload distribution?
[03:06] Sasha: Most production calls are short, 64–256 tokens, but we have occasional 1k–2k long-context retrievals for analyst workflows. We saw a 2x p95 spike when the KV had to fetch cold segments from disk and the model warmed the cache mid-request.
[03:24] Liam: That's expected. Two levers: proactive KV prefetch on request arrival when you can predict prefix patterns, and background async warmers that prefetch based on recent access patterns. For air-gapped environments, we can seed the KV cache at startup with commonly accessed prefixes — that's the 'seed manifest' approach.
[03:40] Raj: How big is that seed typically? For a 4GB model artefact, what's a reasonable prefix size?
[03:47] Liam: It depends on your tail distribution — I'd suggest starting with a 200MB seed covering high-frequency prefixes for the first 100 tokens. The seed reduces cold-starts significantly. We can also tune the KV eviction window.
[03:58] Sasha: And throughput impact? Background prefetch uses CPU and potentially I/O bandwidth — does Redwood's runtime prioritize model inference threads?
[04:07] Liam: Yes, prefetch runs at lower niceness by default; we throttle it to avoid contention. In our config we expose a 'prefetch_budget' and 'io_bandwidth_limit' — for your nodes we recommend prefetch_budget=2 and io_bandwidth_limit=60MB/s for initial tests.
[04:20] Tom: That sounds reasonable.
[04:23] Maya: Moving on to batching — we need to define target latency SLOs so we can select batching windows. Sasha, you said p95 target 400ms for 256-512 seq. What are your throughput expectations?
[04:33] Sasha: For inference API we need ~120 qps steady, burst to 350 during peak with 3-node cluster.
[04:40] Liam: With that target, continuous batching with adaptive windows is good. Proposed defaults: target_batch_latency_ms=20, max_batch_size=64 on the model worker, and a dynamic batcher that scales based on qps. That gives good amortization without violating p95 for short sequences.
[04:55] Raj: Does this change for quantized models?
[04:58] Liam: Quantization reduces per-token compute, which means you can increase batch size before latency tails. But quant also reduces model fidelity; we recommend per-route quant profiles — e.g., 8-bit dynamic for internal intents where slight quality loss is tolerable, and fp16 or int8-fp hybrid for customer-facing responses.
[05:13] Sasha: We need guidance on quant artifacts — do you ship quantized model binaries or tooling to quantize locally?
[05:19] Maya: Both. For air-gapped, we can deliver pre-quantized binaries and a local quant tool if you want to re-quantize. Pre-quantized reduces complexity for the pilot.
[05:27] Tom: Any gotchas around tensor layout or operator kernels on our runtime? We saw a mismatch previously with a CUDA kernel causing wrong output shapes.
[05:36] Liam: We'll vet kernel compatibility. Our runtime auto-selects kernels by architecture and should fallback if an op isn't supported, but in air-gapped installs you need matching kernel modules and libc versions. We'll add a kernel-compat matrix to the manifest.
[05:48] Dana: About audit logs — can you ensure activation and bundle verification events are logged and exported to our SIEM?
[05:54] Priya: Yes, we emit activation events, signature verifications and driver install steps to a local audit log directory. We can provide a syslog forwarder config to ship to your SIEM.
[06:04] Raj: Benchmarks — what microbenchmarks should we run?
[06:07] Liam: We'll supply a bench script that runs three phases: 1) cold-start KV read p95 with seeded vs unseeded, 2) steady-state qps at seq=256 with target batching, 3) long-context stress at seq=1024+ measuring throughput/latency and memory usage.
[06:25] Maya: We'll attach that bench script to the signed bundle. Expect it to be ~10–12 minutes per run.
[06:32] Tom: Regarding checksums — we use FIPS modules for verification. Your signed manifest needs to be compatible with our FIPS validation tools.
[06:40] Maya: We'll run our manifest signing through a FIPS-compatible pipeline and also include a detached signature. If any verification step fails, the installer will halt and log the reason.
[06:50] Sasha: One more question on quant: is there an easy way to rollback quant profiles in production without redeploying artifacts?
[06:56] Liam: Yes — we support model variant routing: the runtime can switch to a different quantized variant or an fp16 variant via the rollout config. That switch is a config-only change if you already have both variants on disk. For air-gapped, you'd need both binaries staged upfront.
[07:10] Raj: Good to know.
[07:13] Dana: From security, we also want the activation to be auditable and revocable. If we revoke a cluster license, what's the time window to deprovision?
[07:21] Priya: Revocation is immediate for active nodes — the local license verifier checks a local revocation list updated during periodic sync windows. For fully air-gapped clusters you can request an emergency revoke token; that still requires you to run the revoke tool locally. We log the revoke event.
[07:36] Tom: How often does the runtime check for revocation?
[07:39] Liam: Default is every 24 hours, configurable down to hourly if you prefer. For pilot set it to 6 hours.
[07:46] Sasha: On operational notes: when we ran with our previous stack we saw a memory spike at long sequences and some OOMs. Any recommendations?
[07:54] Liam: Increase KV chunking and set a max-kv-memory cap to force early eviction; the runtime will fetch on demand. Also offload attention caches to device memory where possible; if device memory is tight, use progressive kv-stealing which keeps working set smaller. We'll propose initial caps in the bench config.
[08:10] Raj: Can you email the exact config blocks we should set?
[08:13] Maya: Yes, we'll include example config snippets in the bundle and an annotated README.
[08:18] Tom: About the bench results — where do we upload them? We can't reach Redwood public endpoints from the airwall.
[08:24] Maya: You can export the bench results as a zipped json and push via your transfer host back to our secure ingest endpoint or share via secure SFTP to the support channel. We'll accept encrypted archives.
[08:35] Dana: Regarding compliance docs — can you share SOC2 attestations and your ISO cert if applicable?
[08:40] Maya: We'll include our SOC 2 type II report and ISO docs in the secure bundle.
[08:45] Sasha: Anything else to watch for when running the bench script?
[08:48] Liam: Ensure the system isn't running extra daemons that could steal GPU memory (eg, misconfigured CUDA tools). Also pin process CPU affinity for the runner to avoid noisy neighbor effects. We'll include a preflight checklist that checks drivers, nvidia-smi output, kernel module versions, and library ABI compatibility.
[09:05] Raj: Great. Let's talk about acceptance criteria for the pilot. We propose: p95 < 400ms for seq=256 at 120 qps, steady throughput within 10% of bench predicted, and successful end-to-end activation within the airwall.
[09:18] Maya: Those are reasonable. Redwood suggests adding a second criterion: successful model variant fallback under simulated pod failures (we'll simulate one node down). That proves graceful degradation.
[09:28] Tom: We can do that.
[09:30] Maya: OK wrapping up, action items recap: I'll send the signed manifest and installer bundle, Liam will push bench script and config, Raj will confirm staging hosts and fingerprint, Sasha will seed a sample artifact, Dana will send security Qs.
[09:44] Raj: Timeline — we aim to start the pilot next week, June 22nd. Is that workable?
[09:49] Maya: Yes, we'll hit the dates in the action items.
[09:52] Dana: One final question: competitors — AltInference told us they can do live quant re-tune but they required outbound connections. With Redwood's airgapped flow that's a non-starter for us. Appreciate the offline tooling.
[10:05] Maya: Thanks. We'll follow up with the checklist and schedule a 30-min checkpoint on June 25th.
[10:12] (call ends)
